title: How Do We Feel About Ella Langley’s ‘Choosin’ Texas’ Setting the Hot 100’s All-Time Record for Weeks at No. 1?
summary: This week's Five Burning Questions looks at Langley etching her name into the Billboard history books with her crossover hit's 23rd week atop the Billboard Hot 100.
contentText:
It’s official: With its 23rd week on top, Ella Langley ‘s “Choosin’ Texas” now reigns alone as the longest-running No. 1 hit in Billboard Hot 100 history.

The country-pop crossover smash breaks its tie with Mariah Carey’s “All I Want for Christmas Is You” on this week’s chart (dated Sept. 26), and most likely isn’t done racking up total weeks. But it’ll face some stiff competition, both short-term from a recently announced deluxe edition release by regular chart-topper Taylor Swift, and then from Carey herself, when the Queen of Christmas looks to reclaim her throne once more this holiday season (and then again in many more holiday seasons to come).

How long do we think Langley will be able to hold onto the Hot 100 record? And what do we think of it as the Hot 100 record-holder, however temporary? Billboard staffers answer those questions and more below.

1. “Choosin’ Texas” breaks Mariah Carey’s 22-week record for longest stay atop the Billboard Hot 100 with her 23rd week at No. 1. Would you rate this a 10 out of 10 in terms of a chart achievement, or does the fact that the record has been tied and/or broken a handful of times already in the past decade change the scope of the accomplishment a little?

Katie Atkinson:  Still a 10 out of 10! The way streaming can track a song’s life for a much longer time than we used to be able to is causing a handful of songs to hang around the top of the chart for longer, naturally, but that shouldn’t downplay the level of hit this specific song is. I’ve been telling my friends who don’t live and breathe the charts: Imagine how long Whitney Houston’s “I Will Always Love You” would have been at No. 1 if we could’ve tracked every time someone played it on their CD at home vs. just counting when they bought that CD or heard it on the radio. Now we can actually see the true longevity of a song’s popularity – and Langley being the first to cross this 23-week threshold shows the unreal staying power of this nearly year-old hit.

Kyle Denis : Rewriting this particular record feels a bit anticlimactic because of how often that’s been done (and attempted!) over the past few years, but it’s still arguably the most important Hot 100 record there is. And for Ella to do this with a solo song as a female country artist is nothing short of impressive. I’ll go with a 9.25.

Melinda Newman : 10 out of 10 for sure! Yes, the methodology for the chart has changed over the years, but, by any measure, this is an astonishing accomplishment. We tend to see longer No. 1 for sure now because of the amended metrics — three of the all-time longest-running No. 1s on the 68-year-old chart are from the last three years — but that doesn’t diminish the feat.

Jessica Nicholson : 10 out of 10. Previous songs that had set milestones for total weeks atop the Hot 100 had not come very close to the total achieved so far by Mariah Carey’s holiday juggernaut “All I Want For Christmas Is You” — much less surpassing it. And for this to be a solo female country artist landing this milestone at a time when women in general continue to struggle to break through in the country music space is a major feat.

Andrew Unterberger : If it’s a tiny bit less than a 10, it’s an insignificant-enough amount less that it’d still round up to 10. This is still one of Billboard ‘s most hallowed chart records, and “Choosin’ Texas” broke it while barely breaking a sweat. And it’s probably not done yet!

2. Based on the social media response to the announcement, it appears that despite the historically lengthy chart dominance of “Choosin’ Texas,” a lot of people are still finding out about the song right now. Is that surprising to you, or is it all just indicative of larger, long-established cultural fragmentation in 2026?

Katie Atkinson:  I guess good for you for not shopping at a Target or watching a single Texas-themed TikTok video over the past 11 months! More than being surprised by people claiming to not know this song, I’m surprised that people feel compelled to share that fact in every comments section. But either way, it’s definitely a symptom of our fragmented culture. Back in the ’90s, it was popular to say you liked “all music except country,” but even the people who said that knew “Achy Breaky Heart” and at least one Garth Brooks song. Now, if you don’t want to engage with country music, your algorithm will make sure you don’t have to. If you truly, somehow, still have not heard this song, I think you’re doing yourself a disservice if you don’t take a listen. Great lyrics, great melody, great vocal – what’s not to like?

Kyle Denis : It’s not surprising at all. For years, especially since the lockdown era of the COVID-19 pandemic, we’ve been talking about the disintegration of the zeitgeist and the splintering of the mainstream into incredibly optimized and hyper-individualized algorithmic silos and digital echo chambers. The tension between the success of “Choosin’ Texas” and how its ubiquity is perceived on an individual level is a natural progression of that discourse. With that being said, I’m sure there are also many people who are, in fact, familiar with “Choosin’ Texas,” but simply don’t recognize it by title or can’t put a face to it.

Melinda Newman : It’s crazy to me that people are still discovering the song around 10 months after it first debuted on the Hot 100 last November (at No. 39), but that just goes to show that cultural fragmentation is alive and well. There are plenty of people who have never listened to country radio who are finding it through pop radio or social media or word of mouth or even through Drake’s languid remake featuring Don Toliver (though Langley’s cameo is now out of the video). You’d pretty much have to be living under a rock to not know the song by now. However, with all the news it’s making for setting the new record this week, there will be people who will check it out for the first time now, for sure.

Jessica Nicholson : It feels like part of the larger cultural fragmentation, given that so many people rely on social media algorithms when discovering new music. There’s no pop artist feature on this track and it leans more squarely in the traditional-leaning side of country music, so it makes sense that some people who don’t often listen to country music haven’t heard the song until now.

Andrew Unterberger : I think it makes sense that there are people who weren’t previously familiar with this song — the same way I imagine my parents probably don’t have any strong memories of Carey & Boyz II Men’s “One Sweet Day” on its way to its then-record-setting 16 weeks at No. 1 in 1995-96. I think it’s fine that some people haven’t heard this song, I just don’t understand why they act like it’s somehow the fault of the song (or of the Hot 100) that it hasn’t made their radar yet. If you don’t pay attention to contemporary pop music or go to any of the places where you’re likely to hear it — or interact with many people who do —  chances are, no one’s going to beat down your door and force you to listen to it!

3. A rising singer-songwriter by the name Taylor Swift is releasing a new deluxe edition, with multiple new songs on it, on Friday. Assuming “Choosin’ Texas” holds on top for a 24th week next week, do you expect that Swift release will interrupt Langley’s run at No. 1 two weeks from now — and will Langley take back over from her soon after?

Katie Atkinson:  “Patient Zero” will definitely halt Langley’s 25th week at No. 1 for at least a week, but I’m going to need to hear the song before deciding what will happen after that.
